records.place: Ostra Vetere and Montecarotto, Castelli di Jesi, Marche

wine.name: Villa Bucci Riserva
wine.appellation: Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva Classico
wine.classification: DOCG since 2010; older vintages were labelled under the Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC
wine.grapes: Verdicchio alone, from old vines of the estate.
wine.sites: Old Verdicchio vines, in the estate's organically farmed vineyards on the limestone and clay hills between Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti, in the historic Classico heart of the Castelli di Jesi.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel, the wine then spends a year to a year and a half in large, long used casks of Slavonian oak, of up to 75 hectolitres, which let it breathe without lending it the taste of wood, and about a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Lemon, almond skin and beeswax with a smoky, nutty depth; dry and rich yet silky, its acidity firm, its finish long and marked by bitter almond.
wine.ageing: Firm and reserved when first poured, it unfolds over several years and lasts for more than ten, drifting towards honey and beeswax.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than ice cold; let a young bottle breathe for an hour, or decant it; a generous glass for white wine.

label.means: The name of the house's Riserva, first made in 1983, when its label could not yet call it a Riserva.
The DOCG of the Riserva since 2010, aged at least eighteen months, six of them in bottle.
Grown in the historic heart of the zone, which the rules set apart from the wider DOC.

records.table: Bucci draws its Villa Bucci Riserva from old vines in the hills between Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti: a Verdicchio raised in big, long used Slavonian casks, never in new wood. Expect almond and a firm, dry line, for this is Verdicchio made to keep.
records.story: Since the eighteenth century the Bucci family has held land in the Castelli di Jesi, with its roots in Montecarotto, one of the walled hill towns that give the zone its name; the estate is a mixed farm, its vines among fields of cereals and olive trees. Ampelio Bucci, who died in 2025 at the age of 89, turned it to bottled wine. The cellar at Ostra Vetere took shape in 1983, and from it came the first Villa Bucci, a Riserva in all but name, for the label could not yet say so. A consultant oenologist worked beside him for decades, and the house held to large old casks of Slavonian oak, which let the wine breathe without tasting of wood. The Verdicchio Riserva of the Castelli di Jesi was made a DOCG in 2010, a name the label of Villa Bucci has borne ever since. In 2024 the estate was sold to Oniverse, the Italian group formerly called Calzedonia, and the family's long tenure came to an end. Verdicchio is so often poured young beside fish; Villa Bucci shows that it can keep and grow for years, like the long lived whites of the north.

others.name: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore
others.note: The estate's younger Verdicchio from the same hills, made to drink sooner than the Riserva.

traps: Villa Bucci names both the estate and its Riserva; the house's younger Verdicchio is the Classico Superiore, a DOC wine, not the Riserva.
The Riserva is a DOCG, Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva, while the zone's other Verdicchio stays a DOC.
Its casks are large and old, so the depth of Villa Bucci comes from old vines and time, not from new oak.

cards.front: In what vessels is Villa Bucci Riserva aged, and why those?
cards.back: Large old casks of Slavonian oak, of up to 75 hectolitres, which let the wine breathe without giving it the taste of wood.

cards.front: When did Bucci make its first Villa Bucci, and what could the label not say?
cards.back: 1983; it was a Riserva in all but name, since the label could not yet call it one.

questions.q: Aged Verdicchio is often expected to taste of vanilla and toast, yet Villa Bucci Riserva shows none. What in the cellar explains it?
opts: Ageing in large old casks of Slavonian oak
A year in new French barriques
Fermentation on the skins like a red
Ageing under a veil of flor yeast
questions.exp: The Riserva spends a year and more in large, long used Slavonian casks, which breathe but give no oak flavour; new barriques would leave the vanilla and toast the guest expected.

questions.q: The Bucci family has held land in the Castelli di Jesi since the eighteenth century. From which hill town of the zone does it come?
questions.exp: The family's roots are in Montecarotto, one of the walled hill towns of the Castelli di Jesi; Cupramontana is where Fazi Battaglia began, and Matelica lies in the separate inland Verdicchio zone.

Istituto Marchigiano di Tutela Vini: Verdicchio

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, and one shared with La Monacesca on the IMT's Verdicchio pages; the group used 30 of 35, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the Riserva is labelled Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva DOCG Classico in the DOCG's years (DoctorWine's and merchants' listings, the IMT's page giving the DOCG of 2010); older vintages were Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC, and Vinous says the first of 1983 could not be labelled Riserva at all.
Founded is left empty with the library: the family's land goes back to the eighteenth century (Vinous and merchants), while the house dates its winery at Ostra Vetere to 1983.

Ampelio Bucci died on 21 August 2025 aged 89 (Gambero Rosso, Sky TG24, Meininger); one source gives his birth as 1936, so he is named with his death and age, not a span of years. The sale of 2024 to the Oniverse group rests on Gambero Rosso, Meininger and Wein.plus; the family behind Oniverse is not named.
The consultant oenologist of nearly thirty years (Vinous, Vinorandum) is described, not named, since no source read gave his dates.

Ageing in cask is given as 14 to 15 months, 18 months and a year and a half to two years by different merchants; the record says about a year and a half (Liberty Wines, DoctorWine). Vine ages of forty to fifty years are on Liberty Wines and Lay and Wheeler.

Library in tension: p-bucci calls the house's plain Classico the unoaked benchmark of the zone, while Liberty Wines has the Classico Superiore part fermented in the same large old Slavonian casks; the record avoids the point.

Left out for want of a second source: the founder's career in fashion and design in Milan, his having no direct heirs, his staying on as an adviser after the sale, and the claim that the Riserva is made only in the best years.

changed: wine.sites: "Old Verdicchio vines, some forty to fifty years of age, in the family's organically farmed vineyards on the hills between"; now "Old Verdicchio vines, in the estate's organically farmed vineyards on the limestone and clay hills between": vine ages move every year and the sources give forty to fifty and fifty to sixty five; since the sale of 2024 the vineyards are no longer the family's; the house gives calcareous and clay soils.

wine.making: "spends about a year and a half in large, long used casks of Slavonian oak, of 50 and 75 hectolitres, which let it breathe without lending it the taste of wood. It rests in bottle before release."; now "spends a year to a year and a half in large, long used casks of Slavonian oak, of up to 75 hectolitres, which let it breathe without lending it the taste of wood, and about a year in bottle before release.": the listings give 12 to 18 months in cask by vintage and casks of 35, 50, 70 and 75 hectolitres; all agree on large old Slavonian casks of up to 75 and on about a year in bottle; steel fermentation is in two listings.
cards[0].back: "of 50 and 75 hectolitres"; now "of up to 75 hectolitres": the same as the making; the front is unchanged.
questions[0].exp: "spends about a year and a half in large"; now "spends a year and more in large": the months in cask vary from 12 to 18 by vintage and source.

questions[1].opts: "Montecarotto, Matelica, Osimo, Ascoli Piceno"; now "Montecarotto, Cupramontana, Staffolo, Matelica": the stem asks for a hill town of the Castelli di Jesi, and Osimo and Ascoli Piceno lie outside it; Cupramontana and Staffolo are towns of the zone, Matelica the inland zone; the key and the stem are unchanged.

questions[1].exp: "one of the walled hill towns of the Castelli di Jesi; Matelica lies"; now "one of the walled hill towns of the Castelli di Jesi; Cupramontana is where Fazi Battaglia began, and Matelica lies": to teach the nearest wrong option of the new set.

story: "For nearly thirty years a consultant oenologist worked beside him"; now "For decades a consultant oenologist worked beside him": a merchant gives nearly thirty years, a writer's account a partnership from 1983 to the consultant's death in 2019; decades is true by both.

story: "sold to Oniverse, a group of wineries, and"; now "sold to Oniverse, the Italian group formerly called Calzedonia, and": wineNews and Wine Couture give the buyer as the Oniverse group, formerly Calzedonia, not a group of wineries.

sources[4]: "Gambero Rosso: the death of Ampelio Bucci, pioneer of Verdicchio"; now "WineNews: Italian wine bids farewell to Ampelio Bucci": wineNews carries the death at 89 and the sale of July 2024 to the group formerly Calzedonia, both facts the record now tells.
open: The founder's birthplace and year (Montecarotto in most accounts, Senigallia in one; 1936 in one); he is named with his death in 2025 and his age.
The consultant oenologist of the house, his years with it and his dates, which rest on a writer's own site; described, not named.
The months in cask by vintage (12 to 18) and the cask sizes (35 to 75 hectolitres); the record gives what all the listings allow.

records.place: Contrada Monacesca, Matelica, Verdicchio di Matelica, Marche

wine.name: Mirum
wine.classification: DOCG since 2010; the plain Verdicchio di Matelica is a DOC
wine.grapes: Verdicchio alone, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: Contrada Monacesca, the estate's own hillside at about 400 metres in the high, landlocked valley of Matelica, which runs north to south between Apennine ridges and is cut off from the Adriatic.
wine.making: Left on the vine some two weeks past ripeness, the grapes are picked by hand in the last third of October. Fermented in stainless steel, the wine spends about eighteen months in steel and six more in bottle before release, with no oak at all.
wine.glass: Acacia, honey, ripe peach and wet stone with summer herbs; broad and dry, its acidity taut, its finish long and closing on bitter almond.
wine.ageing: Tight and slow in youth, it is made to last ten years or more, and honey and breadth come with time.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decanting is not needed, though an hour open does a young bottle good; a big white wine glass.

label.means: Named for the founder, known to all as Miro, as the house tells it.
The inland Verdicchio's DOCG since 2010, aged at least eighteen months before release.
The smaller, higher Verdicchio zone inland, a separate denomination from the Castelli di Jesi.

records.table: Picked late and kept only in steel and bottle, Mirum is La Monacesca's Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva from the closed upper valley inland: taut and stony, with honey and bitter almond, a slower, tighter Verdicchio to set beside the Castelli di Jesi.
records.story: The estate owes its name to monks: in the house's telling, around the year 900 a small band of Benedictines of the abbey of Farfa, driven out by invaders, settled on this hillside above Matelica and built a little church and a monastery, and the place has been La Monacesca ever since. In 1966 the founder, known as Miro, bought the farm, planted its first vineyards and built its first cellar, and the old name of the place became the name of the estate. Its first Verdicchio di Matelica followed in 1973, and the founder's son joined him in 1982. Matelica is the smaller, higher of the two Verdicchio zones, a valley that runs north to south between Apennine ridges and is shut off from the sea, so its wines are tighter and slower than those of the Castelli di Jesi nearer the coast. The house first made Mirum in 1988, picked late from its own hill and dedicated to the founder, and it has worn the DOCG that Matelica's Riserva gained in 2010. Mirum is the inland Verdicchio in full: the grape of the Castelli di Jesi, grown higher, picked later and made to wait.

others.name: La Monacesca Verdicchio di Matelica
others.note: The estate's straight Verdicchio of the valley, the wine it first released in 1973.

traps: Mirum is Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva, from the inland valley, never Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi.
Mirum sees no oak: its depth comes from late picking and long ageing in steel and bottle.
Matelica is the higher, landlocked zone, cooler than the Castelli di Jesi, not the coastal one.

cards.front: Mirum sees no oak at La Monacesca: how, then, is it made to keep?
cards.back: Picked some two weeks past ripeness, fermented in steel, then about eighteen months in steel and six in bottle before release.

cards.front: Who gave La Monacesca its name, in the house's telling?
cards.back: Benedictine monks of Farfa, who settled on the hillside above Matelica around the year 900.

questions.q: A guest wants an inland Verdicchio made to age, and you suggest La Monacesca's Mirum. Which appellation does it carry?
opts: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore
questions.exp: Mirum comes from the closed upper valley of Matelica, the inland Verdicchio zone, and its Riserva is a DOCG; the Castelli di Jesi lie nearer the coast.

questions.q: The founder of La Monacesca bought the farm above Matelica and planted its first vineyards in what year?
questions.exp: The founder bought the farm and planted its first vines in 1966; 1988 is the year the house first made Mirum.

sources.title: La Monacesca: the winery
La Monacesca: Mirum, Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva DOCG
Istituto Marchigiano di Tutela Vini: Verdicchio
Berry Bros. & Rudd: 2021 Mirum, Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva

report: Searches for this record: 3 of the group's share of 35, and one shared with Bucci on the IMT's pages; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the house's own Mirum page gives Verdicchio alone and no source read ties Chardonnay to Mirum (the estate grows a little Chardonnay for another wine), so the record says Verdicchio alone; if older vintages held some Chardonnay, no source read says so.
First made in 1988: a merchant's account and the house's anniversary bottling of 1988 to 2018 (a blend of vintages, not a 1988 wine).
The founder is described, not named: the house names him and his nickname Miro, but no source read gave his dates; his son, who joined in 1982 and leads the house, is living and not named.

The monks of Farfa around the year 900 are the house's account and are told as such; the house also claims Matelica's DOC of 1967 as the first in the Marche, which the record leaves out, since the Rosso Conero DOC dates from the same year.
Making by the house's sheet: some two weeks of overripening, picking in the last third of October, steel fermentation, eighteen months in steel and six in bottle; merchants confirm steel and no oak.

Left out for want of a second source: the parcel of about three hectares of old vines and its heavier clay (one merchant each), the bottle counts and the claim that Mirum is made only in great vintages.

changed: story: "of the abbey of Farfa, fleeing the Lombards, settled"; now "of the abbey of Farfa, driven out by invaders, settled": the house names the Lombards and a merchant's account the barbarian invasions; the Lombard kingdom had fallen in 774, more than a century before, so the record keeps what both accounts allow.
open: The founder's son joining in 1982 rests on the house's page as the author read it; not in the refuter's results.
Around the year 900 (the house) or the tenth century (a merchant's account) for the monks; told as the house's account.

records.place: Castelplanio, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico, Marche

wine.name: Titulus
wine.appellation: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico
wine.classification: DOC, from the historic Classico heart of the zone
wine.grapes: Verdicchio alone, hand picked in the house's own hillside vineyards.
wine.sites: The house's own hillside vineyards in the historic Classico zone of the Castelli di Jesi, in the hills around Cupramontana, where it began, and Castelplanio, its seat.
wine.making: The hand picked grapes are chilled and macerated briefly in the press, then softly pressed. The must ferments in stainless steel at 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, and the wine rests about four months on its fine lees, for crispness, before bottling.
wine.glass: Pale straw with green glints; apple, pear, broom flower and aniseed, then a dry, tangy palate of medium body and a finish of bitter almond.
wine.ageing: Drink it young, in its first years after the vintage, while the apple and aniseed are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, with no decanting, in a white wine glass of middling size.

label.means: The house's Verdicchio Classico, sold in the green amphora bottle with a scroll tied at its neck.
The DOC of the hills behind Ancona, named for the walled hill towns around Jesi.
A wine of the zone's historic heart, the part the rules set apart from the wider Castelli di Jesi.

records.table: The green amphora chosen by a design competition of 1953 is the bottle that carried Verdicchio abroad, and Titulus, Fazi Battaglia's Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico, is the wine that wears it. Young and cold suits it: crisp and unoaked, with apple, aniseed and bitter almond.
records.story: Fazi Battaglia began in 1949, when two families, the Fazi and the Battaglia, joined to make wine in a small cellar at Cupramontana, a hill town of the Castelli di Jesi. A few years later the Angelini family of Ancona took it over, led by the founder of a pharmaceutical company who was also mayor of Ancona, and set out to make its little known Verdicchio recognisable at a glance. In 1953 the house announced a competition for a bottle, and a Milanese architect won it with a curving, emerald green amphora drawn from the wine vessels of the Etruscans, a scroll rolled and tied by hand at its neck. In 1956, by the accounts of two merchants, the house moved to a larger cellar at Castelplanio, where it has stayed. The amphora became the signature of Verdicchio abroad, and in America it was nicknamed after an Italian film star. Titulus is the Verdicchio Classico that wears it: fermented in steel, rested on its lees and bottled young, it is the wine inside a single house's bottle that came to stand for a whole appellation.

others.name: San Sisto
others.note: The house's Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva Classico from its San Sisto vineyard, a fuller wine than Titulus.

traps: The amphora is Fazi Battaglia's own bottle of 1953, not a rule of the appellation; Verdicchio is sold in ordinary bottles too.
Titulus is a Classico DOC, not the Riserva, which is a separate DOCG of the Castelli di Jesi.
The house was founded by two families, the Fazi and the Battaglia, not by one family of that double name.

cards.front: Which two families joined in 1949 to begin Fazi Battaglia, and where?
cards.back: The Fazi and the Battaglia, in a small cellar at Cupramontana in the Castelli di Jesi.

cards.front: How is Titulus made, from the press to the bottle?
cards.back: Hand picked Verdicchio, chilled and softly pressed, fermented in steel at 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, then about four months on its fine lees.

questions.q: Has Titulus, the Verdicchio Classico of Fazi Battaglia, seen any oak on its way to the bottle?
opts: No: steel, then about four months on fine lees
Yes: a year in new French barriques
Yes: eighteen months in large Slavonian casks
No: it ages under flor like a Fino
questions.exp: Titulus is fermented in stainless steel at low temperature and rests on its fine lees for about four months; the long months in large Slavonian casks belong to a Riserva such as Villa Bucci.

questions.q: In 1953 Fazi Battaglia held a competition for the bottle Titulus wears. What did the winning amphora draw on?
opts: The wine vessels of the Etruscans
The glass flasks of Roman Ancona
The straw covered flasks of Chianti
questions.exp: The Milanese architect who won drew his curving green amphora from ancient Etruscan wine vessels; the straw covered flask is Tuscany's, a different bottle with a different story.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages (fazibattaglia.com) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the competition of 1953 won by a Milanese architect stands on the house's page, Profile Wine Group and Vinotria; the move to Castelplanio in 1956 stands on Xtrawine's producer page and a second merchant's profile (Vinoscout's, by the search summary), with the house's address at Castelplanio, so it is hedged as the merchants' account.

The architect is named on the house's page but no source read gave his dates, so he is described; the Angelini founder of the pharmaceutical company and mayor of Ancona is described for the same reason.

Ownership told only as history with years where sourced: Meininger and WineNews report a sale of Fazi Battaglia to Bertani Domains, the Angelini wine group, but the year was not clear in the summaries read, so the record leaves it out for the refuter.
The nickname after an Italian film star in America rests on two importers' pages; the star is living and not named.
The San Sisto Riserva appears as Fazi Battaglia San Sisto in older listings (Vinissimus) and as Tenute San Sisto in recent ones (Xtrawine); the change of label is reported, not dated.

Left out for want of a source: what the word Titulus means to the house, a first vintage of Titulus under that name, the house's vineyard area and the amphitheatre vineyard above Cupramontana (one merchant).

changed: story: "when two families of Cupramontana, the Fazi and the Battaglia, joined to make wine in a small cellar in that hill town of the Castelli di Jesi."; now "when two families, the Fazi and the Battaglia, joined to make wine in a small cellar at Cupramontana, a hill town of the Castelli di Jesi.": the sources put the cellar at Cupramontana and say nothing of where the two families came from.

others[0].note: "The house's Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Riserva, a fuller wine than Titulus, labelled in later vintages as Tenute San Sisto."; now "The house's Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva Classico from its San Sisto vineyard, a fuller wine than Titulus.": the Riserva has been a DOCG under that name since 2010 and comes from the house's San Sisto vineyard; Tenute San Sisto appears on another of the house's wines, so it is no label change of this one to teach.
open: The year the Angelini family took the house over, and the dates of the industrialist and of the architect; both described.
The move to Castelplanio in 1956 rests on three secondary accounts and no page of the house's the refuter read; one source dates the bottle's design to 1954.
Tenute San Sisto as a later name on the house's labels, for the integrator.

wine.name: Cùmaro
wine.classification: DOCG since 2004, the Riserva level above the Rosso Conero DOC
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, by the house's sheet; the DOCG allows up to 15 per cent Sangiovese.
wine.sites: A vineyard on the edge of Osimo, facing south east at about 150 to 200 metres, on very deep, chalky loam over old marine deposits, inland of the limestone headland of Monte Conero.
wine.making: Harvested by hand into boxes, usually in October, the grapes are destemmed, lightly crushed and left to ferment on their native yeasts in steel at 27 to 29 degrees Celsius for 12 to 14 days, then go through the malolactic. The wine ages 12 to 14 months in barriques, part of them new, and some months in bottle.
wine.glass: Fresh and dried cherry, plum and a balsamic lift over damp earth and sweet, savoury oak, in a deep ruby wine; full and plush, its tannin firm but ripe, its acidity fresh.
wine.ageing: It can be opened a few years after release, yet a cool cellar keeps it for years, and it grows more savoury there.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; give it an hour in a decanter while young, and a large red wine glass.

label.means: From komaros, the Greek word for the strawberry tree, which by the house's account gave Monte Conero its name.
The DOCG of the headland's red since 2004: at least 85 per cent Montepulciano and two years of ageing.
The DOC of the same hills, since 1967, a younger wine than the Riserva.

records.table: Montepulciano from a south east facing vineyard at Osimo, inland of the limestone headland above Ancona, makes Cùmaro, Umani Ronchi's Conero Riserva, aged in barriques. Here is the Marche in red: deep and plush, cherry scented with a balsamic lift, a wine to decant and pour with meat.
records.story: Umani Ronchi carries the name of its founder, who in 1957 set up a small farm at Cupramontana, in the heart of the Verdicchio Classico zone. In 1968 two entrepreneurs, a man and his son in law, took the farm over, kept the founder's name and, by the house's account, refounded it as a wine estate on 4 January; a year later its seat moved to Osimo, south of Ancona and inland of the Conero, where its Rosso Conero cellar opened. The house began to sell abroad in 1973, and in 1983 made its first Casal di Serra, a Verdicchio from a single vineyard. Cùmaro followed in 1985, made to show what Montepulciano could give on the deep chalky soils by Osimo, and named from the Greek word for the strawberry tree that, the house says, gave Monte Conero its name. In 2001 the house began to farm an estate near Roseto degli Abruzzi, beyond the Marche in the Abruzzo. The Riserva of Rosso Conero became the Conero DOCG in 2004, and Cùmaro took the new name. The Marche is not only Verdicchio, and Cùmaro is the proof: Montepulciano by the Adriatic, ripe and dark yet fresh.

others.name: Casal di Serra
others.note: The house's Verdicchio of the Castelli di Jesi from a single vineyard, first made in 1983.

others.name: Pelago
others.note: A Marche Rosso IGT of Cabernet Sauvignon, Montepulciano and Merlot.

others.name: San Lorenzo
others.note: The house's Rosso Conero DOC of Montepulciano.

traps: Cùmaro is Montepulciano, the grape; it has nothing to do with Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, the Sangiovese of a Tuscan town.
Conero Riserva is the DOCG; Rosso Conero is the DOC of the same hills, a younger and separate wine.
Umani Ronchi is the name of the founder of 1957, kept by the family that refounded the house in 1968; it is not a place.

cards.front: What Greek word lies behind the name of Umani Ronchi's Cùmaro?
cards.back: From komaros, Greek for the strawberry tree, which by the house's account named Monte Conero.

cards.front: Umani Ronchi first made Cùmaro in which year, and from which grape?

questions.q: By law, which grape must lead a Conero Riserva such as Umani Ronchi's Cùmaro, and by how much?
questions.exp: The Conero DOCG asks at least 85 per cent Montepulciano with up to 15 of Sangiovese, and Cùmaro is Montepulciano alone; a blend with much more Sangiovese is nearer Rosso Piceno.

questions.q: Two entrepreneurs, a man and his son in law, took over a small farm of Cupramontana in 1968, refounded it as a wine estate and kept its founder's name. Which house?
questions.exp: They took over Umani Ronchi, the farm its founder had set up in 1957, and kept his name; Fazi Battaglia began in Cupramontana too, but in 1949, by a union of two families.

Umani Ronchi: Cùmaro, Conero Riserva DOCG
Istituto Marchigiano di Tutela Vini: Conero Riserva
Grape Collective: Umani Ronchi of the Marche and Abruzzo
Enolike: Umani Ronchi, the winery

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages and leaflets were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the seat at Osimo (the house's address and Enolike, which says it moved there a year after 1968), the founding of 1957 at Cupramontana and the refounding of 4 January 1968 (the house's history; Grape Collective), Cùmaro's first vintage of 1985 and its Conero Riserva DOCG (the house's Cùmaro page and leaflet); one house leaflet gives the early 1950s for the start, and the record keeps the house history's 1957.

The Conero DOCG of 1 September 2004, the Rosso Conero DOC of 21 July 1967, the minimum of 85 per cent Montepulciano and the two years of ageing are from the IMT's Conero Riserva page and disciplinare.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose: the son in law who refounded the house in 1968 and later led it, and his son, who joined in 1990 and runs it, for people.json; the building contractor of 1968 and the founder of 1957 are described, since no source read gave their dates.

records.place: Ascoli Piceno, Rosso Piceno Superiore, Marche

wine.name: Roggio del Filare
wine.classification: DOC; the Superiore from a smaller zone within the province of Ascoli Piceno
wine.grapes: Montepulciano, about seven tenths, with Sangiovese for the rest, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyards at Castorano, at about 200 metres in the hills of the southern Marche near Ascoli Piceno, within the smaller zone the Superiore requires.
wine.making: The grapes ferment in temperature controlled stainless steel with about four weeks on their skins; the wine then ages some eighteen months in new barriques before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Intense ruby turning garnet with age; ripe cherry, blackberry and plum with vanilla, tobacco and dark chocolate from the oak and a touch of lavender; full and warm, its tannin ripe, its finish long.
wine.ageing: Generous enough to drink within a few years, it keeps for several more as the oak melts into the fruit.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a large red wine glass, after an hour in a decanter if the bottle is young.

label.means: The Rosso Piceno DOC from a smaller southern zone near Ascoli, aged at least a year before release.
The house's name for its oak aged Superiore, first made from the 1993 vintage.

records.table: Velenosi blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese from the hills near Ascoli Piceno for Roggio del Filare, its Rosso Piceno Superiore, and gives it eighteen months in new barriques. The result is ripe, dark and warm, cherry and plum under vanilla and tobacco: the southern Marche's Montepulciano at full stretch.
records.story: Velenosi was founded in 1984 at Ascoli Piceno, the historic city of the southern Marche, by two very young entrepreneurs whose surname it carries. Brecciarolo, a Rosso Piceno Superiore of Montepulciano and Sangiovese from vineyards at Offida and Ascoli Piceno, goes back to the house's first years in the 1980s. The Rosso Piceno DOC had been created in 1968 for the reds of the Marche's southern hills, blending Montepulciano with Sangiovese, and its Superiore comes only from a smaller zone within the province of Ascoli Piceno and is aged at least a year. A second Superiore, Roggio del Filare, followed in 1993: the same two grapes from its vineyards at Castorano, with about four weeks on the skins and eighteen months in new barriques. The business became a limited company, Velenosi Srl, in 2005. Where the Conero gives Montepulciano nearly alone on its limestone headland, the Piceno blends it, and Roggio del Filare is that southern blend in its ripe, oak dressed form.

others.name: Brecciarolo
others.note: The house's older Rosso Piceno Superiore, Montepulciano with Sangiovese from Offida and Ascoli Piceno, made since its first years in the 1980s.

traps: Rosso Piceno blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese, while Conero is Montepulciano nearly alone, so the two are not one style.

Roggio del Filare and Brecciarolo are both Velenosi's Rosso Piceno Superiore: Roggio, first made in 1993, is the one given new barriques.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 35, one of them on the IMT's domain finding nothing on Rosso Piceno; the house's own pages were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the founding of 1984 (the house's page, Arquilla Wines and other merchants; Bottle of Italy alone says the late 1980s), Roggio del Filare's blend of about seven tenths Montepulciano with Sangiovese, its eighteen months in new barriques and its first vintage of 1993 (the house's page, Callmewine, Xtrawine), and its appellation Rosso Piceno DOC Superiore (the house).

The Superiore's zone of thirteen communes, its further ageing in wood and the DOC of 1968 are from the Consorzio Vini Piceni's page; the region record's Montepulciano 35 to 85 per cent with Sangiovese 15 to 50 agrees with it.

The house's page puts the vineyards at Castorano, while merchants say Offida and Ascoli Piceno at about 200 metres on calcareous clay; the record follows the house and leaves out the soil and altitude.

The four weeks of maceration in steel rest on Callmewine and Bottle of Italy; the tasting notes are theirs too, and the serving temperature follows the Codex's reference for a full red (merchants give 16 to 18 and 18 to 20).
Living names met, none in the fragment: the two founders, the partner of 2005 and the founder's children who now work in the house, for people.json.
Left out for want of a source: what the words Roggio del Filare mean, the picking date, the house's Offida reds and whites, the counts of hectares and estates, and its awards.
